title: Why Trend Following Still Works in Tough Markets - Systematic Investor - Ep.381

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Why Trend Following Still Works in Tough Markets - Systematic Investor - Ep.381.docx

summary: Top Traders Unplugged year-end panel part two with ten systematic managers. Topics: total portfolio approach, long volatility, process stability, drawdown nature of CTAs, high-vol products and 2026 predictions. Conclusion: do not change trend models after pain, 2023-25 drawdown was volatility compression, and CTA allocations are far below optimal.

coverage.note: intro, disclaimers, agenda; AI and TPA questions posed
TPA for CTAs, AI use, CTA allocation sizing
big-picture diversification, Sharpe of S&P, long vol
financialization thesis, whether pain justifies change
replication model, slower and simpler outperformed
owning decisions; CTA drawdowns vs other hedge funds
hit ratio, paper on drawdowns, mean reversion of performance
drawdown depth, perception of risk, when trend earns
ETF drawdown views, allocator manager selection behaviour
retail high-vol product joke, Kelly, return stacking

completeness_estimate: 0.60 - the first reader caught the main TPA, process-stability, drawdown-structure and Sharpe/vol-compression arguments; it missed the AI-use remark, several allocator-behaviour mechanisms (narrative, iron spine, ETF drawdown visibility, no-single-event drawdowns, long vs deep), the Katie, Yov and Andrew 2026 predictions, and misattributed two C03 claims and the Barclay-vol statement.

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: even if you expect your sharp ratio of your other portfolio to be one and a half and you think that CTAs are uh.5 sharp then in order to maximize your sharp you need to
claims.claim: Mean-variance optimisation across a total portfolio implies a very large CTA allocation (about 1/3 of risk) even if CTA Sharpe is only 0.5 versus 1.5 for the rest, because of CTA diversification.
claims.direction: raise CTA/trend allocation to ~1/3 of risk
claims.conditions: assumes zero correlation to the rest of the portfolio and stable Sharpes

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: In practice flows follows performance and that will be the most determining factor of flows into the CTA universe.
claims.claim: Flows into CTAs are driven by past performance rather than by portfolio-theory arguments such as total portfolio approach (TPA), so TPA is unlikely to change CTA allocations much.
claims.testable: partly - flows vs trailing performance can be tested

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: you should think about CTAs in the context of the asset classes that you're holding in your own portfolio. So if you're if you're a fixed income manager, you should think about fixed income CTA.
claims.claim: CTA exposure should be chosen to hedge the allocator's existing asset-class exposure (fixed-income holders want fixed-income CTA, equity holders something different).
claims.direction: match CTA sleeve to existing holdings
claims.testable: partly - conditional hedge benefit can be measured

claims.speaker: Allan (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: you get much more allocation to CTA macro commodities when you optimize in the context of the overall portfolio because you're going to have less allocation to long short equity and credit
claims.claim: A hedge-fund portfolio optimised within the total portfolio (GIC / JP Morgan AM paper) tilts to CTA, macro and commodities and away from equity long-short and credit, which duplicate factors already held.
claims.direction: long CTA/macro/commodity hedge funds; less equity L/S and credit
claims.testable: yes - optimisation in the cited paper

claims.speaker: Allan (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: it it does TPA already. it it it it evaluates the markets and assesses where are the best risk adjusted returns where where the best opportunities
claims.claim: A trend-following programme already behaves like a total portfolio approach because it dynamically allocates risk to the markets with the best risk-adjusted opportunity rather than holding static weights.

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: there aren't many things you have out there that have zero correlation to stocks and bonds and do well when you need it the most um that you can scale and do in liquid fashion
claims.claim: Managed futures is nearly the only scalable, liquid strategy with zero correlation to stocks and bonds that pays off in stress, so a strategic allocation would be around 25%.
claims.direction: long managed futures ~25% of strategic allocation
claims.testable: partly - correlation and crisis-alpha measurable; 25% is a judgement

correction.issue: Speaker likely wrong: the host only introduces Jim at the end of C04 ('I certainly need to hear from Jim') and Jim starts with 'Yeah, look to take a step back'. The C03 speaker (agrees with Yov, cites the 6% US hedge fund allocation) is a different panelist, probably Andrew, and the transcript does not name him.
correction.fix: Unnamed panelist (not Jim; possibly Andrew): managed futures is almost the only scalable, liquid strategy with zero correlation to stocks and bonds that pays off when needed, so a strategic allocation would be about 25%; pod shops come close but not as scalable.

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: a typical institutional um allocator in the US has about a 6% allocation to hedge funds today of which managed futures according to kind of the broad classification of hedge funds is sub 10%.
claims.claim: US institutions hold about 6% in hedge funds, of which managed futures is under 10%, i.e. about 50bp of the portfolio, far below optimal; career risk and benchmark anchoring prevent raising it to ~30% of the hedge-fund sleeve.
claims.conditions: benchmarked to hedge fund indices

correction.issue: Same speaker problem as C03-3: attributed to Jim but the host brings Jim in only after this speaker finishes. Also the 30% figure is the managed futures share of the hedge fund sleeve ('from a 6 or 7% allocation to a 30% allocation which is where it should be'), which the claim states but attributes to Jim.
correction.fix: Unnamed panelist (not Jim): US institutions hold about 6% in hedge funds with managed futures under 10% of that, roughly 50bp of the portfolio; benchmarked to hedge fund indices it is career-risky to raise managed futures from 6-7% to about 30% of the hedge fund sleeve, which is where it should be.

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: what do you think the sharp ratio is of the S&P over the last 125 years?
claims.claim: Allocators rarely know long-run Sharpe ratios (S&P and 60/40 about 0.35 over 125 years), yet 95% of investors rely on stock/bond mixes whose diversification benefit is overstated; true diversification needs non-asset strategies like trend and long volatility.
claims.direction: favour non-correlated strategies over stock/bond diversification
claims.conditions: stocks and bonds are highly correlated in the tail
claims.testable: yes - long-run Sharpe and correlation computable

correction.issue: Overstates what was said about diversification: the speaker says stocks and 60/40 each have a Sharpe of about 0.35, i.e. adding bonds gives zero diversification benefit, and calls the stock/bond approach zero diversification, rather than merely overstated.
correction.fix: Jim: no allocator he asks can name the 125-year Sharpe of the S&P or of a 60/40 portfolio (both about 0.35), so bonds added no Sharpe benefit over stocks; yet 95% of investors diversify by holding more correlated assets, whereas true diversification comes from non-asset strategies such as trend following and long volatility.

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: the one thing that tons of academic research points to is the one thing that is a true uh consistent diversifier and the most important thing in portfolio is is a long volatility hedge
claims.claim: Academic research identifies a long-volatility hedge as the one consistent diversifier and most important portfolio component.
claims.direction: long volatility
claims.testable: partly - depends on hedge implementation cost

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: the brakes give you control. The brakes allow you to slow down into the turn and accelerate out. You win races. You go faster by having V in the portfolio.
claims.claim: Long volatility is like brakes on a race car: although it earns about zero in the long run, it lets the portfolio keep risk on in the straights and so raises geometric performance, rather than merely slowing it.
claims.direction: hold small permanent long-vol and add into risk
claims.conditions: use the payoff to monetise by adding risk afterward
claims.testable: partly - needs rule for re-risking after payoff

claims.speaker: Rich (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: what a stable process does do it doesn't eliminate the draw downs but it does prevent panic and behavioral drift.
claims.claim: A stable, pre-committed process does not remove drawdowns but prevents panic and rule changes made in response to recent outcomes, which is a main investor mistake.

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: We have actually a pretty good ability to predict distribution. predicting direction is hard.
claims.claim: Distribution width and tail fatness by regime (volatility) are forecastable while direction is not, so trend-model choice should be driven by a forward view of the return distribution and supply/demand factors rather than by backtest optimisation.
claims.testable: partly - vol forecastability is well documented; mapping to trend speeds is untested

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: you know, tell us all the changes you've made in your model and the answer is none. Zero. Not a line of code, not an instrument.
claims.claim: A trend replication model left unchanged for ten years gives a track record that is fully consistent; the best outcome for an allocator is that the manager never needs changes, because it is hard to know whether changes help going forward.
claims.testable: partly - consistency of track record can be judged; change value unknowable

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: the reason why we have seen the underperformance in the last few years is not because the model doesn't work is because we've seen this compression that we're talking about. We have seen just less outliers.
claims.claim: Recent CTA underperformance is explained by fewer outsized trends (compression), not by model breakdown; diagnose by measuring the Sharpe extracted from markets that trended at a given underlying Sharpe versus history, which is roughly unchanged.
claims.indicator: Sharpe captured per unit of underlying market trend Sharpe
claims.testable: yes - decomposition of returns into trend availability and capture

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: about 70% of the of the volume in the front front month contract are CTAs Okay, to me that's a warning sign.
claims.claim: A market where CTAs account for ~70% of front-month volume (SORA/Ionor example) is financialized; a manager selling non-financialized risk factors should drop it, since the thesis of the product is trading what others do not.
claims.indicator: share of front-month volume attributable to CTAs
claims.direction: exclude crowded markets from non-financialized trend programme
claims.conditions: applies only if product thesis is low beta to the financialized universe
claims.testable: partly - volume share data hard to obtain

claims.speaker: Nick (CTA replication researcher)
claims.quote: I would say no. Is the pain an invitation to think about changing the model? Maybe.
claims.claim: Drawdowns are a prompt to review for blind spots but not a reason to change the model, especially when the underperformance is explained by repeated V-shaped reversals (yen, Liberation Day).

claims.speaker: Nick (CTA replication researcher)
claims.quote: the replication model almost has an assumption on how the average underneath behaves. And as long as that remains through time, you don't really have to change your your your recipe
claims.claim: A replication of the CTA index need not change when underlying managers change models, as long as their changes net out and managers do not become too fast for the replicator to track.
claims.indicator: CTA replication tracking error vs index
claims.conditions: assumes manager changes average to zero
claims.testable: yes - tracking error against index measurable

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: over the past 3 years slower and simpler has worked better
claims.claim: Over the past three years slower and simpler trend models outperformed more complex or faster ones; allocators should ask managers to own design decisions that cost return in this regime.
claims.direction: long slower, simpler trend
claims.conditions: 2023-2025 regime of high dispersion

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: the reason why CTAs tend to lose money is mostly um because nothing happens
claims.claim: CTA drawdowns come from nothing happening (whipsaw and volatility compression) rather than from a single event, as the strategy is like buying straddles paid via trading costs.
claims.conditions: low realised-trend, low vol periods

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: you don't actually need 50% of your markets to be winners, you just need maybe 40% of your markets to be winners to have a good positive year.
claims.claim: A trend portfolio needs only about 40% of markets to be winners for a good year because winners are outsized; drawdowns arise when winners drop to 30-35%.
claims.indicator: percentage of markets with winning trades

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: vault compression and the percentage of winners has just shrunk below the break even point and that's something that we have seen in the last in the last 3 years
claims.claim: Over 2023-2025 volatility compression pushed the share of winning markets below break-even, causing the industry's multi-year drawdown.
claims.indicator: volatility compression; fraction of winning markets

claims.speaker: Katie (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: what we find is if you look at what's happening during a lot of our very challenging environments they tend to be pretty good environments for equities
claims.claim: Managed futures drawdowns tend to coincide with calm, equity-friendly, low-volatility environments, and recoveries are faster in challenging equity environments because the hit ratio rises.
claims.indicator: managed futures drawdowns vs equity regime
claims.testable: yes - paper on largest managed futures drawdowns

claims.speaker: Katie (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: usually that's followed historically by one or two years of very positive performance.
claims.claim: After a very challenging period for managed futures, one or two years of strong performance has typically followed, so timing manager tops and bottoms is trend-following-trend and not advisable.
claims.direction: hold through drawdowns
claims.conditions: longer-horizon mean reversion vs short-horizon persistence

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: 16% draw down over 25 years like it's child's play compared to equities.
claims.claim: Managed futures maximum drawdown is about 15-16% over 25 years, much smaller than equities, so perceived risk exceeds actual risk.

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: you're going to go through like the space is going to make money a lot of money when the world changes a lot right
claims.claim: Trend following earns most when the world changes a lot (inflation shocks, regime shifts over ~24 months) and struggles in noisy markets where little actually changes, which is what total portfolio allocators with static assumptions do badly.
claims.conditions: big change in information; fails in noise without regime change

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: a typical allocator who is not as well versed in statistics of no persistence of alpha and a wide dispersion is will tend to um oversell a a given an individual manners outperforms
claims.claim: With wide manager dispersion and no persistence of alpha, allocators chase the recent winner with a brand name and oversell it, creating a negative feedback loop when it underperforms.
claims.testable: yes - persistence of CTA manager returns

claims.speaker: Rob (systematic trader)
claims.quote: even if we run that at sort of half Kelly, we we could be running at sort of annualized risk of sort of 40 50%.
claims.claim: A Sharpe-1 strategy run at half Kelly implies roughly 40-50% annualised volatility, so high-vol CTA products are feasible and could be sold to retail at higher fees as a proportion of vol (offered half in jest).
claims.indicator: Sharpe ratio, Kelly fraction, volatility target
claims.direction: scale volatility up to half Kelly
claims.conditions: assumes Sharpe near 1 and positive skew

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: I wouldn't say leverage as much as capital efficiency right the the return stack
claims.claim: Higher interest rates make capital efficiency (return stacking, portable alpha, yield stacking) valuable again, so growth in 2x/3x and stacked ETFs reflects a need to do more with less capital, not a desire for more risk.
claims.conditions: after zero-rate era

claims.speaker: Katie (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: the Barkley uh CTA index were running at an annualized volatility of between 20 and 25%. And since then it's gone down and actually in the last few years we are now below 5%
claims.claim: The Barclay CTA index volatility fell from 20-25% in the 1980s/early 1990s to below 5% in recent years as institutions entered and assets grew.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the Barclay CTA index volatility figures (20-25% in the 1980s and early 1990s, below 5% now) are stated by the host Neils, interjecting after Katie. Katie only supplied the explanation that institutions entered and assets grew.
correction.fix: Host Neils: the Barclay CTA index ran at 20-25% annualised volatility in the 1980s and early 1990s and is below 5% in recent years; Katie (preceding remark): institutional adoption and larger assets pushed managers toward lower-risk, size-management programmes.

claims.speaker: Allan (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: you want more risk will give you more equities whereas in fact you should have a balanced portfolio and then decide how much leverage to apply to it
claims.claim: Wealth portfolios should hold a balanced, diversified portfolio and then apply leverage to reach the desired risk, rather than adding equities for risk.
claims.direction: balanced portfolio plus leverage

claims.speaker: Allan (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: so I think next year will be the year of the bond breakout. So, US 10ear yields up to 6% and then down to 3 and a half%.
claims.claim: Prediction that US 10-year yields rise to 6% and then fall to 3.5% in 2026.
claims.direction: long volatility in rates

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: That 2026 will in a lot of ways look like 2022. Uh the pain trade will be market down and interest rates up.
claims.claim: 2026 resembles 2022 with stocks down and rates up as the pain trade, because investors hold stocks with long-vol band-aids and bonds as diversifier; VIX and implied vol hedges could pay.
claims.direction: short equities, short bonds, long VIX

claims.speaker: Mark (CTA manager)
claims.quote: You're going to see higher inflation, which means higher uh yields on uh on treasuries.
claims.claim: 2026 view: higher inflation raises Treasury yields, credit crises carry over from 2025, MAG 7 bubble bursts pulling equities down, and Europe resurges.
claims.direction: long Europe; short MAG 7, bonds

claims.speaker: Neils (host)
claims.quote: the Fed the Fed will end up having to hike rates uh next year at least once.
claims.claim: Prediction that the Fed has to hike at least once in 2026 despite political pressure.
claims.direction: short bonds

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: generally the approach has been very cautious on our side. Um it is able to help us in coding.
claims.claim: A CTA manager uses AI cautiously: it helps with coding, summarising client discussions and the team's own thinking, and as a test of message clarity (an AI misreading a presentation shows where the message is unclear), but it is not presented as a source of alpha.
claims.conditions: cautious adoption; coding and summarisation uses
claims.testable: no - process practice, no measurable claim

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: And then CTAs get like 2% where they make a zero difference to the overall portfolio in terms of convexity, in terms of diversification.
claims.claim: Bucket-style hedge fund allocation (fixed slices for macro, long/short, real estate, private credit) leaves CTAs with about 2%, too small to change the total portfolio's convexity or diversification; looking at the whole portfolio instead is what would raise the CTA weight.
claims.direction: larger CTA weight under whole-portfolio view
claims.conditions: depends on allocator process (silo vs total portfolio)
claims.testable: partly - allocation weights observable, benefit simulable

claims.speaker: Allan (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: do they look through that or do they have to adjust for that in terms of their own views as well.
claims.claim: Caveat to TPA: if the investment team makes tactical views and also allocates to hedge funds that already make tactical bets, it is unclear whether they look through those managers' positions or adjust for them, so TPA double counts or conflicts with manager-level tactical risk.
claims.conditions: when hedge fund tactical bets overlap with the allocator's own tactical views
claims.testable: no - open question the speaker leaves unresolved

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: breaking that anchoring mechanism and having people kind of start with a blank sheet sheet of paper
claims.claim: The real benefit of TPA for CTAs is that it can break allocators' anchoring to hedge fund indices and legacy bucket sizes, forcing a statistical blank-sheet allocation; but much of TPA is theatre to win broader mandates, so the speaker is only cautiously optimistic.
claims.direction: higher managed futures allocation if anchoring breaks
claims.conditions: benchmark and career risk anchor allocators to hedge fund index weights
claims.testable: no - qualitative view about institutional behaviour

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: that again didn't exist until 1985 and doing it simply because of recency bias uh and a lack of needing to really manage risk and understand risk in a meaningful
claims.claim: Most of the investment world runs a simple long-only stock and bond mix whose structure only dates from about 1985, and it persists through recency bias and because the long falling-rate era removed the need to manage risk, so its apparent diversification is untested in a different regime.
claims.conditions: a different rate/inflation regime would expose the lack of risk management

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: I'm not able to make money. I'm going to drift away from that space. That's actually going to be very bad. You're just going to lose your investors.
claims.claim: A manager who sells a specific trend style (for example fast trend) should not drift away from that style when it underperforms, because style drift defeats the reason the investor hired them and loses the investors; model changes should follow the stated thesis, not recent pain.
claims.conditions: applies when underperformance in the chosen style is explainable by the environment

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: if everybody goes to a 15-day model, it's not going to be a surprise, right?
claims.claim: A legitimate reason to revisit a trend model is evidence of industry-wide drift (for example all managers moving to 15-20 day models), which would be visible against a benchmark or replication; absent such evidence of a structural deviation, underperformance alone does not justify changes.
claims.indicator: industry average trend speed vs own model
claims.conditions: change only if structural deviation is understood and persistent
claims.testable: partly - industry speed drift measurable via index replication

claims.speaker: Nick (CTA replication researcher)
claims.quote: is the objective to minimize track and error probably not because obviously the outperformance is important
claims.claim: A replication or benchmark model need not minimise tracking error to the CTA index, since outperformance matters; high tracking error in a given year does not by itself show the model works or fails.
claims.testable: partly - tracking error and excess return vs index measurable but the speakers state no conclusion

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: CTA drawdowns are much more difficult because there isn't necessarily a one event that will explain the draw down
claims.claim: Because a CTA drawdown has no single event to blame (unlike a discrete bet gone wrong), allocators find it harder to explain to an investment committee and to stay patient, even though the cause is systematic (volatility compression, too few winning markets).
claims.conditions: applies to CTA drawdowns from lack of trends rather than event losses

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: in CTAs you don't necessarily see a very deep draw down but you might have a go through a situation where for a long period
claims.claim: CTA drawdowns are typically long rather than deep: volatility compression makes outsized trends hard to harvest for an extended period without a single deep loss, which answers the host's question of whether long or deep drawdowns are worse for the strategy.
claims.conditions: volatility compression regime
claims.testable: yes - drawdown depth/duration of CTA indices measurable

claims.speaker: Katie (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: it's very difficult to pick a winning manager in any one year
claims.claim: Fund-of-funds studies show it is very difficult to pick the winning CTA in any single year and strategies on average recover after drawdowns, so short-run performance persistence is weak and mean reversion over longer horizons dominates; dispersion drives behavioural errors.
claims.testable: yes - persistence of manager returns testable

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: bonds had didn't have a draw down for 20 years basically and now you've had a 15 16% draw down
claims.claim: Bonds went about 20 years without a meaningful drawdown and then suffered a drawdown of 15-16%, similar in size to the maximum drawdown of managed futures over 25 years, which undercuts the view that CTAs are riskier than traditional assets.
claims.indicator: bond index drawdown vs managed futures max drawdown

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: equities are down 50%. What are you going to do with your portfolio where you're all in on the AI trade across
claims.claim: Portfolios are concentrated in the AI trade across equities, rates and other holdings; a year later with equities down 50% a trend programme that cuts losses and can go short would be the protection, so the case for CTAs is that the world may change sharply after a quiet, noisy period.
claims.direction: trend following protects in an equity bear
claims.conditions: trend benefits from large regime shifts, suffers in noise
claims.testable: partly - crisis-alpha of trend in equity bears testable

claims.speaker: Jim (volatility specialist)
claims.quote: But a lot of allocators want to hear that you have a like an iron spine.
claims.claim: Trend followers cut losing positions rather than holding with a white-knuckle grip, but many allocators want a narrative of conviction (an iron spine, such as buying Bitcoin at 20,000 because it would recover), so the strategy's disciplined loss-cutting is hard to sell.

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: no, people don't like draw down. They don't like it because you can see it every day. You can see it every minute.
claims.claim: In an exchange-traded wrapper the price and drawdown are visible every day and minute, so investors react to drawdowns more than in a monthly-reported fund; drawdowns do matter to ETF holders.
claims.conditions: applies to daily-priced ETF vehicles

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: honesty and equivocation actually plays against the broader adoption of
claims.claim: Allocators trained to buy the dip look for a story that explains a rebound after a drawdown, but financially sophisticated CTA managers honestly say they do not know it will rebound (they have exited the losing positions and will find new trends), and this honesty works against wider adoption.

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: if you can get people to focus on this as a strategic long-term allocation and and basically get them focused on day one not on the gears and how they work
claims.claim: To make managed futures a standard allocation, present it as a strategic long-term holding judged by its benefit to the overall portfolio instead of model details such as lookback lengths or number of positions; the speaker expects this to be tested over five years.

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: the big money is is are the people who are riskaverse and and who spend 80% of their me mental energy how to avoid being embarrassed
claims.claim: The large pool of money in managed futures products is risk-averse allocators focused on avoiding embarrassment, not leverage-seeking retail; niche ETF structures (return stacking, buffered, covered call) can still reach multi-billion scale (an ETF firm sold for about $2 billion).

claims.speaker: Katie (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: it's going to be great when it goes up just like Bitcoin and it's going to be terrible when it goes down
claims.claim: A daily-liquid high-volatility CTA product cannot smooth its prints as private equity does, so it will attract performance-chasing inflows after good runs and then disappoint investors in drawdowns, as with Bitcoin; old-school high-vol CTAs avoided this because there was no daily ticker.
claims.conditions: applies to daily-priced, high-volatility products

claims.speaker: Allan (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: they go through exceptional periods raise some assets they have a draw down lose a lot of assets it repeats.
claims.claim: High-volatility trend managers (a long-standing example is Mulvaney) have a repeating cycle of exceptional years, asset raising, deep drawdown and asset loss, so a high-vol ETF version would probably follow the same flow cycle; institutions had moved to low-vol trend, with some swing back to high-vol launches.

claims.speaker: Katie (CTA researcher)
claims.quote: rates go lower over stimulation of the US economy and we could things could look awesome and then suddenly things could fall apart.
claims.claim: 2026 prediction: a boom-and-bust roller coaster, with rates falling and over-stimulation of the US economy making conditions look strong before things suddenly fall apart; 2026 could be a pivotal year for the macro change seen in 2025.
claims.direction: boom then bust
claims.testable: no - view with little supporting reasoning

claims.speaker: Andrew (replication ETF manager)
claims.quote: I think institutions start buying ETFs in the managed future space.
claims.claim: 2026 prediction (self-described low probability, high significance): institutions begin buying managed futures ETFs, as most institutional allocators hold a hedge fund analyst mandate and look for hedge funds rather than ETFs.

claims.speaker: Yov (CTA manager)
claims.quote: Equities up 25%. Uh that will make me happy. Uh but I'm afraid I'm kind of uh I'm kind of in the camp of 6% 10 year rate uh most likely.
claims.claim: 2026 view: equities up 25% would be the speaker's wish, but the more likely outcome is a 10-year Treasury yield of about 6%.
claims.direction: 10-year yield up to about 6%
